summary:
Macau is a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China, standing under the national framework of the Basic Law while administering its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1996, the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offences identically, and no provision criminalises gender expression. The general age of consent is 14 for both homosexual and heterosexual sex; Penal Code Article 166 separately prescribes 3 to 10 years' imprisonment for anal intercourse with a person under 14, and up to 4 years where a 14-to-16-year-old's inexperience is taken advantage of.

There is no legal pathway to gender recognition. The Identification Services Bureau maintains no policy for changing the sex marker on Macau identity cards, and the gender-marker-change study carried out in 2015 never produced legislation. Between 2004 and 28 February 2026 the Bureau received eight written requests to change the gender marker on identity documents and rejected all eight. On 7 April 2026 the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) stated that legal recognition of gender identity still requires "prudent study" of core societal values, civil law and family relations, and that there are "no plans to revise the framework"; a 31 March 2026 appeal by four trans residents had not altered that position. Macau is the only area in China without either identity-card gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions, both of which are available in mainland China and in Hong Kong.

The document mismatch has direct border consequences: a trans man holding a Hong Kong identity card marked male remains registered female in Macau, producing confusion when crossing the boundary.

The Basic Law's Article 25 list of protected grounds omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Statutory non-discrimination protection is sectoral, extending to employment under Article 6(2) of Law No. 7/2008, with fines of up to MOP$50,000 per affected worker, and to personal data under Law No. 8/2005 and the ombudsman's mandate under Law No. 4/2012.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. A March 2013 bill tabled by Legislative Assembly member José Pereira Coutinho to grant same-sex civil unions the rights available to heterosexual couples was rejected 17 votes to 1 with 4 abstentions and expressly excluded the right to adopt. Same-sex couples, and households headed by same-sex couples, remain ineligible for some legal rights available to opposite-sex couples.

Domestic-violence protection excludes same-sex partners. A 2011 public consultation had included "same-sex cohabitants in an intimate relationship" in scope, but the government's 2012 concluding report removed the reference citing "a lack of social consensus", and the 2016 legislation insisted on the exclusion on the ground that same-sex partners were not considered family members. Rainbow of Macau lodged a complaint with the UN Committee against Torture in October 2015; the Committee's 2015 concluding observations urged Macau to protect all domestic-violence victims "without discrimination". The UN Human Rights Committee noted in 2017 that Macau still does not permit transgender people to change gender markers on birth records and identity documents.

Public expression around LGBT people is constrained by stigmatising coverage. On 9 June 2015 the newspaper Exmoo headlined a report on an alleged sexual offence with a slur against gay people, prompting Rainbow of Macau spokesperson Jason Chao to restate that the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offenders identically.
tangentialFactors:
Organised LGBT advocacy in Macau is recent and thin: the Macau LGBT Rights Concern Group was created in late 2012 and Rainbow of Macau registered in April 2013, and gay culture in the territory remains mostly invisible. The first organised push for gender recognition dates to February 2015, when Rainbow of Macau met Identification Bureau officials with one individual, a transgender student using the pseudonym Avery, speaking behind a screen; Avery had told Macau media that month about abuse and bullying experienced at a local school.

Official statements have at times signaled medicalising attitudes toward gender and sexuality. On 16 August 2018 the deputy director of the Education and Youth Affairs Bureau (DSEJ), Leong Vai Kei, said that students with "indications of homosexuality" would be referred to doctors or psychologists for medical examination; she later apologised, claiming misquotation and mistranslation from Cantonese.

Macau's position compares unfavourably with the rest of China on recognition: mainland China and Hong Kong both permit gender-marker change and sex-reassignment provisions, while Macau permits neither, and its non-discrimination grounds remain narrower than the sectoral protections its own employment, data and ombudsman statutes provide.
localsOnly:
Employment is the one domain where residents hold an enforceable non-discrimination right covering sexual orientation: Article 6(2) of Law No. 7/2008, with fines of up to MOP$50,000 payable for each affected worker. Personal data complaints fall under Law No. 8/2005 and maladministration complaints under the ombudsman's mandate in Law No. 4/2012, but neither statute is framed around sexual orientation or gender identity as a protected ground.

Residents seeking a gender-marker change must apply to the Identification Services Bureau, which has rejected every one of the eight written requests filed between 2004 and 28 February 2026 because no data-change policy exists. Legal Affairs Bureau and Justice Services Direction positions recorded in April 2026 confirm no revision is planned pending study of core societal values, civil law and family relations.

Same-sex partners are excluded from domestic-violence legislation as non-family members, so a resident leaving a violent same-sex relationship has no recourse under that statute; this exclusion survived the 2011 consultation, the 2012 report and the 2016 enactment despite the UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations and Rainbow of Macau's October 2015 complaint.

Same-sex couples and their households remain ineligible for some rights available to opposite-sex couples, and adoption is not available to them following the 2013 civil-union bill's rejection and its express exclusion of adoption rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Macau's Penal Code or other statutes contain hate-crime or hate-speech enhancement provisions covering offences motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity; the stigmatising press material cited here evidences public hostility but not a charging or sentencing rule.

No sourced material addresses access to gender-affirming care in Macau, including whether hormone therapy or surgery are available, lawful, or reimbursed, nor whether prescriptions issued abroad are honoured.

Facilities and screening questions are unresolved: nothing in the sources states how Macau handles gendered toilets, detention cells, airport or border screening, or security pat-downs for trans travellers, beyond the identity-card mismatch noted above.

Whether Macau recognises foreign same-sex marriages, foreign civil unions, or foreign court-ordered name and gender changes for residents or visitors is not sourced here.

The circumstances of the 2015 gender-marker-change study, including its authors and its actual recommendations, are not detailed in the available material; only its outcome, no enacted law, is established.

Enforcement practice under Law No. 7/2008 in cases alleging sexual-orientation or gender-identity discrimination is unverified: no complaint counts, outcomes, or penalty records appear in the inventory.
